claims.claim: A below-knee prosthetic leg can range from about $3,000 to $70,000 or more depending on features, so a billed price reaching fifty thousand dollars is real for sophisticated devices.
claims.episode_span: A finished below-knee prosthesis can reach a billed price of fifty thousand dollars
claims.source_title: How Much Does a Below-Knee Prosthetic Leg Cost? - Celerity Prosthetics
claims.supporting_quote: Depending on the features and quality, a below-knee prosthetic leg could range from $3,000 to $70,000 or more

claims.claim: The materials for e-NABLE's 3-D-printed body-powered Raptor Hand cost approximately $35.
claims.episode_span: a 3-D-printed body-powered hand can be produced for under fifty dollars in filament and fasteners
claims.supporting_quote: The cost of materials of the Raptor Hand is approximately $35.

claims.claim: Traditional professionally made prostheses can cost thousands of dollars per year, which is why e-NABLE targets underserved recipients.
claims.episode_span: yet commercial equivalents still list for several thousand because the clinical delivery channel has not changed
claims.supporting_quote: e-NABLE typically focuses on underserved communities (including children missing hands) for whom traditional prostheses are too expensive (because they can cost thousands of dollars per year) or impractical (because children outgrow them).

claims.claim: Children outgrow prosthetic devices, making traditional prostheses impractical for them and forcing repeated replacement.
claims.episode_span: The same pattern appears in simpler body-powered hands that children outgrow every year
claims.supporting_quote: traditional prostheses are too expensive (because they can cost thousands of dollars per year) or impractical (because children outgrow them).

claims.claim: Medicare Part B covers prosthetic devices only when ordered by a doctor or other health care provider, pays only suppliers that participate in Medicare, leaves the beneficiary paying 20% of the Medicare-approved amount, and some states require prior authorization for certain lower-limb prosthetics.
claims.episode_span: Insurance and Medicare reimbursement schedules further lock the workflow in place: payment is tied to documented clinical encounters rather than to the delivered hardware alone
claims.supporting_quote: Some states may require prior authorization for certain types of lower-limb prosthetics before Medicare will pay.

claims.claim: The FDA defines an external limb prosthetic component (ankle, foot, hip, knee and socket components; mechanical or powered hands, hooks, wrists, elbows and shoulders) as a medical device that, assembled with other components, constitutes a total prosthesis.
claims.episode_span: Regulatory overhead is modest for standard sockets and body-powered components, which sit in the lightest device class
claims.supporting_quote: An external limb prosthetic component is a device intended for medical purposes that, when put together with other appropriate components, constitutes a total prosthesis.

claims.claim: External limb prosthetic components are FDA Class I (general controls) devices exempt from premarket notification (510(k)), so the regulatory burden on socket and component makers is at the lightest tier.
claims.episode_span: Regulatory overhead is modest for standard sockets and body-powered components, which sit in the lightest device class
claims.supporting_quote: Class I (general controls). The device is exempt from the premarket notification procedures in subpart E of part 807 of this chapter

claims.claim: Commodity polypropylene traded at about US$1.21 per kilogram in North America in August 2026, so a socket's few kilograms of thermoplastic represents only a few dollars of material.
claims.episode_span: The socket itself uses a few kilograms of commodity thermoplastic worth only a few dollars in total
